Approved the G1051 maintenance-release forward-port design: separate approved operations per downstream destination, evidence-backed already-applied outcomes, and no production rewind.

responses.filter_design:7:1: fixed: specify ancestry and exact merged-PR evidence, independently approved already-in-history/previously-merged outcomes, explicit no-diff-unproven block, recheck/race limits, recovery and real-Git/provider tests.

output.summary: Handle no-diff maintenance forward-ports as evidence-backed, separately approved non-mutating outcomes, or block clearly if history cannot establish inclusion. Preserve source records, report exact observed Git/PR evidence and do not claim an unperformed merge.

Both independent re-reviews accepted the evidence-backed no-diff forward-port handling, including separately reviewed non-mutating outcomes and a clear block where equivalence is unproven. No open findings or notes remain to filter.

The independent implementation re-review accepted both earlier corrections and identified one new material correctness finding: release recovery can select an unrelated historical merged PR and block the currently approved release. It reopens implementation. There are no non-material notes to filter.

findings.text: Add a real-Git/provider regression for release PR recovery with an earlier PR from the same branch already merged at H, subsequent approved release tip T descending from H, and a later finish. Assert the old PR is ignored and a new PR at T merges successfully. Also cover exact-head recovery when an older unrelated PR is listed first, while retaining the current tests that an unapproved descendant merged after T is recorded and blocks propagation.

responses.review_impl:2:1: fixed: select an exact-head merged PR first, ignore historical heads that do not descend from the approved tip, and preserve the mismatch block for merged descendants.

output.summary: Recovery now prefers a merged PR at the exact approved tip and only considers a different head when it descends from that tip; older unrelated merged PRs no longer prevent a new delivery. A real local Git/provider reproduction now completes the later approved release, and all four required head-race and nested-lineage tests pass.

not: A ceremony framework: every mechanism must prevent a real failure worth its cost.
A second source of truth beside Git.

Inherently opinionated: it ships an opinionated default graph, but every opinion (graph, lenses, prompts, policy) can be customised by the project.
principles: Git is the store; state is visible and repairable by hand.

Guard against drift at both levels: from what a goal asked for, and from the project's original intent. A goal that departs from the project's intent is flagged when it is added, and the owner either changes the goal or amends the intent.
Prefer deleting to adding; keep prompts distilled.

output.summary: The no-diff forward-port cases distinguish reachability, proven historical PR merges and unproven equivalence without fabricating a merge.

findings.impact: Unapproved code can reach production and be propagated as though the owner approved it.
findings.text: plugins/zzzops/zzzops/engine/ops/lines.py:167-177 and 283-284: an already-merged PR is accepted before its head is compared to the approved T, and merged-PR recovery accepts any head descending from T. The subsequent checks verify the merge base and source but not that the merged head was T. In a real-Git/fake-provider local reproduction I approved T, paused finish immediately before provider pr view, pushed H on the release branch, externally merged that PR, and resumed finish. Production contained H and finish proceeded to request forward-port approval instead of reporting divergence. This defeats the design’s exact-head approval binding and permits automatic propagation after an unapproved head is merged. Verify merged PR head/merge parent against T on both already-merged and recovery paths, and stop for human review on mismatch; cover this race with a provider fixture.

findings.impact: Valid nested maintenance releases cannot be forward-ported to their intended downstream branches.
findings.text: plugins/zzzops/zzzops/engine/forward_port.py:91-95: common ancestry checks only the maintenance line’s immediate source commit and its direct parents. For a legitimate nested maintenance 2.1.1 based on a finished 2.1 whose own work includes multiple commits, production/dev can share the verified released 2 baseline while neither the 2.1 tip nor its immediate parent is an ancestor of the destination. Forward-port is then incorrectly refused as lacking verifiable common released ancestry. Follow recorded release provenance to a verified common released ancestor rather than stopping at one Git parent; add an end-to-end nested-maintenance forward-port case.

findings.impact: Legitimate release finishes can become permanently blocked by an unrelated historical pull request, even though the approved new head is valid and ready to merge.
findings.text: plugins/zzzops/zzzops/engine/ops/lines.py:298-307: recovery now selects the first merged PR returned for the release head and production base regardless of its head. If an earlier PR from the same release branch was already merged and subsequent work produced a new approved T, that historical PR is neither the PR to recover nor evidence of an external merge of T. Nevertheless verified_merged_pr blocks on its different head before the code can find or create the actual PR for T. This affects ordinary releases too, and the prior logic excluded such older heads. Distinguish an unrelated historical PR from a candidate for the current approved delivery: find exact-head matches first, only treat a changed-head merge as a divergence when it is demonstrably the current delivery, and preserve the race protection. Add coverage for a stale previously merged PR followed by a fresh approved tip.

output.summary: Both prior findings are corrected and their focused tests pass, but the revised merged-PR discovery introduces an unrelated historical-PR recovery regression.
The actual external-merge, nested lineage and invalid-snapshot regressions exercise real Git; the focused run correctly remains red on a source-goal cycle.

spec:
Support inserting a release between existing ZzzOps target releases, so a patch release can be planned and delivered without renumbering later work. The motivating example is targeting a patch release such as 2.1; target releases must no longer be restricted to integers. This is useful for shipping a ZzzOps fix as a patch while later releases are already planned.

Acceptance criteria:
- Let an owner insert, target and work toward an appropriately ordered release such as 2.1 alongside existing integer releases. Existing goals assigned to later releases remain assigned to those releases unless explicitly changed. A patch release can use the existing release workflow and gates.
- Define and validate release identifiers and their ordering explicitly. Avoid treating version-like identifiers as floating-point numbers: for example, 2.10 and 2.1 must not silently collapse into the same identifier. The supported identifier grammar and how it relates to actual semantic versions are design choices to surface to the owner if not already decided.
- Integrate the identifier through the actual engine, goal schema, CLI, default workflow, release and branch handling, scheduling, display, validation, docs and compatibility boundaries wherever relevant. Do not assume a particular release-branch naming scheme without checking existing policy.
- Preserve existing integer release data and goal histories; do not silently reorder, rewrite or repurpose existing releases or production branches. Analyze how existing repositories and in-flight goals adopt the new version; report unrelated broken migrations for a separate goal rather than expanding scope to repair them.
- Cover identifier parsing and ordering, insertion with later targets already present, scheduling, release cutting and completion, compatibility with existing integer goals, invalid and ambiguous input, branch/CLI behavior and mixed engine versions using realistic local Git/remote fixtures. Run focused real-engine checks first, followed by appropriate integration checks.

Constraints: ZzzOps release support is a branching strategy, not an automatic deployment or package-publishing service. Respect existing owner approvals and policy choices. Do not create a real release, change production branches, publish artifacts or change other goals' release assignments as part of capturing this goal.

Owner clarification: releases can always be inserted by adding another dot-delimited numeric component. For example, after 2.1 exists, insert 2.0.1 before it, then insert 2.0.0.1 before 2.0.1: 2 < 2.0.0.1 < 2.0.1 < 2.1. Support arbitrarily nested finite component sequences rather than imposing a fixed version depth. Trailing-zero forms representing the same value, such as 2 and 2.0, are equivalent; 2.1 and 2.10 remain distinct. Design and test ordering, canonical identity, branch naming, insertion, compatibility and safe patch-line ancestry at nested depths.

GitHub protected-merge clarification: use an explicitly approved immutable source snapshot and GitHub’s protected pull-request merge checks, including the supported expected-PR-head guard, for this delivery. Do not claim that the PR merge atomically verifies an independent source or goal ref. A real GitHub check established that GraphQL updateRefs atomically validates an unchanged source ref while changing an unprotected destination, but GitHub rejected this direct mutation when the destination required an approving PR review; mergePullRequest exposes expectedHeadOid but no separate expected source ref. Preserve normal PR approval and branch protections; do not bypass them. Do not require or implement optional live-source cross-ref transaction mode in this delivery; leave such stricter enforcement for a future goal on providers or workflows proven to support it. Test and document the remaining snapshot/revocation limitation honestly. The user chose to continue after this finding.
title: Allow inserting patch target releases between planned releases
